The Coil-Supply Report Rebuilt on Current Findings

§1 — What the report says that is no longer true

The coil-supply model, from JT-60SA to ITER is the project's report. It was last assembled on 19 October 2026. Since then the fast-discharge breaker model, the PF winding capacitances, the VS3 circuit and the reading of the 22HLVN fast-discharge column have all changed, so several of its headline numbers are now wrong rather than merely old. This section is the review that found them, made on 20 October 2026 against the plan records and the register. Each row names the section that replaces the claim.

§3 — Each coil's worst windows across the fifty scenarios

The coil-set estimates of §4 cannot run every scenario switched, so they run the windows that load each supply most. This section chooses them from the 50 complete DINA scenarios that the scenario screen already reads. It uses DINA's demand only to place the windows; nothing about the circuit comes from DINA.

The selection extends its owner rather than forking it. power_convertor.scenario_loading.ranked_windows and its driver scripts/iter/scenario_loading.py already build the current, voltage-limit fraction, dI/dt, zero-crossing and bridge-mode-transition measures over the same complete DINA census, and rank windows by them. This section adds the two criteria they lack, initiation with the switching-network insertion and the fastest VS1 swing, and a per-supply window file. For each of the thirteen supplies, select one window per applicable criterion:

  • the largest |I|, which also sets the fast-discharge trip current for §5;
  • the largest voltage demand as a fraction of the converter limit;
  • the largest |dI/dt|;
  • plasma initiation with the switching-network insertion (CS modules, PF1, PF6);
  • the fastest VS1 swing (PF2–PF5, VS1);
  • current zero crossings and the transfers between one-bridge, two-bridge and circulating operation, at the 10 % and 40 % bands of rated current.

Windows within 1 s of each other in the same scenario merge. Each window carries its scenario, start time, criterion, criterion value and the averaged state it starts from.

  • data/iter/scenario_loading/coil_set_windows.json (main checkout) lists every supply with at least one window per applicable criterion. Ties break by the stated rule: the larger criterion value, then the earlier scenario number.
  • The census record docs/research/iter-coil-set-census.html opens with the window table, an HTML table rather than an image, and one figure. That figure draws each criterion's values over the 50 scenarios as a grey population, with the selected windows highlighted, saved under docs/figures/coil-set-census/.
  • Negative control: a synthetic scenario with a spike injected into one coil's dI/dt is selected for that coil and criterion and for no other coil.

§4 — The coil set through its worst windows: ripple, edges, resonances and detector pickup

Run every §3 window on the integrated switched model that iter-switched-terminal-transients §6 assembles. All supplies switch together on one composed plant (shared-coil-supply-model §4), on the republished windings, at installed-loss bounds, with both converter forms as arms. This section adds the windows and the measures; it does not build a second integrated model. The §7 filter candidates the reassessment keeps run as further arms on the windows of the supplies they serve.

Each measure family is computed by its existing owner, called on the new windows:

  • ripple lines, peak-to-peak and the neutral grounding current by scripts/figures/coil_circuit_playback.py (neutral_current, spectrum), as scripts/iter/cs_switched_window.py already calls them;
  • the first turn and the exterior turns by scripts/iter/first_turn_voltage.py and exterior_turn_voltages.py;
  • driven modes and their quality factors by scripts/iter/winding_damping.py and frequency_response_prediction.py;
  • detector pickup by scripts/iter/quench_detection_pickup.py (pickup_detector, and the detector's hold_response from src/power_convertor/ripple_margins.py).

The census is a window loop in the integrated run's own caller, scripts/iter/integrated_simulation.py, not a fifth implementation of any measure.

For each coil and window it measures:

  • Ripple: terminal lines from 6f to 24f, the 500 Hz carrier and its sidebands, and the 1.6 kHz front-end line, across the coil and to ground; peak-to-peak terminal ripple; current ripple; and the neutral grounding current against the 0.1 A earth-fault detector minimum.
  • Fast edges: terminal dV/dt; the first-turn peak; the worst section's peak to ground; and the largest voltage between adjacent sections against the 152 V helium Paschen minimum, as an exposure prompt rather than a verdict.
  • Resonances: each coil's driven winding modes and their quality factors at both loss bounds, and their distance from the 300 and 600 Hz thyristor lines, the 500 Hz carrier and the 1.6 kHz front end, with the line-to-section gain at the nearest line.
  • Quench-detection pickup: the PF bridge and CS tape signals through the detector front end of QD pickup §3, against the threshold and hold time, as a margin.

The record gives one scorecard row per coil. Each row holds the worst value of each measure, the window and arm it came from, its reference from the IDM register, and the margin. Where the register holds no reference the row says so, and no margin is filled from another component. DINA's coil voltage is compared and reported as a deviation, never as a pass mark.

Done when:

  • Every supply's scorecard row is complete in docs/research/iter-coil-set-census.html, with figures for ripple lines, edges, mode-line proximity and detector margin under docs/figures/coil-set-census/, each rendered and inspected.
  • Step convergence: halving the step moves no reported peak by more than 1 %. A window that does not converge is drawn and tabulated as drafted, with its measured movement.
  • Negative control, the one iter-switched-terminal-transients §6 declares: each coil's 600 Hz current ripple with the passive coupling disabled, divided by its ripple with the coupling in place, equals |Zscreened|/|Zbare| at 600 Hz to within 5 %. A second control: a supply whose converter is held idle shows only the coupled pickup, below its driven ripple.

§5 — Fast discharge of every circuit on the current FDU

Re-solve iter-switched-terminal-transients §8's discharges of every circuit, every group and all together on the library FDU. The re-solve goes through the owners scripts/iter/fast_discharge.py, scripts/iter/tf_fast_discharge.py and scripts/iter/vs1_discharge.py, which call fast_discharge_unit.py and discharge_resistor.py rather than stamping their own breaker. The FDU's elements:

  • vacuum breakers that open at their own current zero;
  • the counter-pulse capacitor;
  • the pyrobreaker and its stray;
  • the snubber at the register's attachment, with XK23KG's attachment as a second arm until tf-cold-test-validation §4's cold-test-commutation-observables node says which attachment the measured commutation supports;
  • two FDUs in series on CS1, one per module, and one FDU on every other PF and CS circuit (778SPD v1.0 §1.2; register row "Fast discharge units per circuit");
  • the heated resistor on the cold-test law.

Every PF and CS trip follows the PF/CS FDU interlock sequence (Figure 3-19 of the PF/CS FDU description, carried into the IDM register):

  • the bypass switch opens about 320 ms after the command;
  • the vacuum breaker is commanded at about 420 ms and opens about 22 ms later;
  • the counter-pulse fires 8 ms after it opens;
  • the current reaches zero 6–10 ms after that.

So the resistor is inserted about 0.45 s after the trip command, and the coil current flows through the bypass and the breaker until then. 778SPD caps the whole breaker delay at 0.5 s. Time zero is the trip command. Front quantities are measured from the breaker's contact separation, and currents and energies at the breaker's own current zero, not at the command.

X7TDMM v2.0, the approved FDU local I&C description, governs the sequence. G96SWS v1.1's faster sequence runs as a sensitivity arm: bypass at about 280 ms, its check-back at about 350 ms, and the zero check-back at 25–30 ms.

The converter's state during the delay is IDM's (register row "PF/CS FDU interlock time sequence"). At the quench trigger the converter goes to inversion, or to freewheeling, rather than being blocked, and the PMS closes later but before the breakers open (7NFVWB v1.0 p. 5; 778SPD v1.0 §3.2). The reference arm is therefore inversion at the converter's inversion limit from the trip until the PMS closes, then freewheeling through the PMS until the breaker separates. IDM gives no PMS closing time, so it is run at both ends: early, and just before the breaker separates. The bound arm is the converter blocked and the coil freewheeling from the trip. That bound is the upper limit on the interrupted current when a disruption is driving the coil current up, and inversion is the design case.

No owner models the converter through the delay yet. fast_discharge.py and vs1_discharge.py hold it as a fixed bypass resistance and insert the resistor directly. This section therefore adds the delay as a stage of the fast_discharge.py owner, ahead of the FDU insertion:

  • the converter as a voltage source at its registered inversion limit from the trip;
  • a PMS make switch that closes at the stated time and shunts the converter;
  • freewheeling through the PMS until the breaker separates;
  • for the bound arm, the PMS closed from the trip.

If the shared ConverterNetwork must carry these elements, that change goes to converter_units.py's owner as a followup and the stage stays in the owner script until then.

Each case trips from two currents: the supply's rated current, and the largest current §3 found for it in the scenarios. Every PF and CS row is run in four arms. That includes the PF2–PF5 discharges that vs1_discharge.py runs with the VS1 converter connected across them, because those trips go through the same PF FDUs and the same interlock. VS3 is normal-conducting and has no FDU, because 778SPD v1.0 §1 and §1.2 assign FDUs only to the superconducting coils (register row "Fast discharge units per circuit"). So it has no row here. The four arms:

  • the reference arm with the PMS closing early;
  • the reference arm with the PMS closing just before the breaker separates;
  • the blocked bound arm;
  • the reference arm on G96SWS's faster sequence.

For each circuit and arm the record gives:

  • the resistor peak against its group's 778SPD transient-inclusive pair, read from the supply register: at main-breaker and pyrobreaker operation, TF 8.5/10, CS 6.5/7.0, PF1 and PF6 7.0/7.0, PF2–PF4 7.5/8.0 and PF5 6.5/7.3 kV (register row on the per-group limits). For the CS rows the judged quantity is the full FDR terminal voltage, resistance and inductance together. The reference FDR inductance in every row is tf-cold-test-validation §13's per-section mild-steel model from 48NZDV's prototype TF module (scripts/mctb/fdr_inductance.py, record tf-cold-test-fdr-inductance). It is scaled to each FDR through S9BRS4's modules in series and sections in parallel, with the external bus separated as 7JQSNL's 3 µH cable. CS and PF FDRs take the remagnetisation regime, the conservative case. TF takes the residual regime its unipolar FDR rests in, with remagnetisation as an arm. Scaled this way, the CS and PF units land at 0.73–0.91 of 7LDTQA's rows across 6–45 kA, so 7LDTQA's table, with steel buses, runs as the upper-estimate arm. Both tables are energy secants, Ls = 2W/I², read through the FDU library's SecantInductance, so the terminal voltage carries the incremental inductance Ld = W′(I)/I = Ls + (I/2)·dLs/dI on the resistor branch's own current. The constant 94.9 µH end is reported beside them as the upper bound. The record states that the 48NZDV values were read by eye from plots and S9BRS4's by OCR, and the rows cite them as such;
  • the quasi-steady I·R against the 22HLVN column;
  • the transient to ground against the transient reference the register names;
  • the across-coil, worst-section and first-turn peaks;
  • the energy per unit against 778SPD's maximum;
  • τeq against the group limit;
  • the counter-pulse margin: the counter-pulse ring current's peak against the breaker current at contact separation, after the delay, which says whether the breaker's current zero is reached. The current at separation is what the counter-pulse must interrupt, and it can exceed the current at the trip when a disruption drives the coil current up during the delay.

TF runs on the cold-test posterior passive mode, and keeps its instantaneous insertion. X7TDMM's sequence belongs to the PF/CS FDU, and the register holds no interlock timing for the TF FDU. The MCTB cold-test sequence of about 0.21 s (GJ4JX4 v1.2) is a test-bench sequence, so it is not carried to ITER here. The TF rows state that the delay is not modelled.

§6 — Whether disruptions must be run to qualify the FDUs, and the cases if so

None of the 78 held DINA cases is a disruption: all are normal pulses or first-plasma cases, and the screen and every fast-discharge row so far trip the FDU from a steady current with the plasma's flux frozen. A disruption differs in three ways that bear on an FDU:

  • The current quench drives every coil through −dψp/dt, so a coil's current can rise above its reference while the breaker is still to open. The breaker must then interrupt a larger current than the rated one, and its counter-pulse circuit is sized to create a current zero at a stated current.
  • The induced EMF adds to the I·R across the resistor and to the voltage to ground while the FDU is inserted.
  • The plasma's magnetic energy couples into the discharging circuits and adds to the energy each resistor absorbs, against 778SPD's per-unit maximum.

IDM does not treat a trip coincident with a disruption as an FDU design or qualification case. The resistors are sized on the operating scenarios and on single-coil tests, and the load specifications keep disruptions and fast discharge apart. Yet the PF specification allows a fast discharge at any time in nominal operation. 3M9D27 tabulates disruption-induced coil current changes of up to 9.4 kA on PF2 and 5.05 kA on each CS1 module, while the breaker, counter-pulse and pyrobreaker are rated on coil current alone (register row "Fast discharge coincident with a plasma disruption", cae6e45d). The combined case is therefore a margin IDM does not compute. The recommendation is a bounded set of cases, not the whole disruption database. Decision disruption-cases, relocked on 21 October 2026 to the trip-first cases below, fixes the scope, and the decision block carries the relock and its rationale. Gate g-csrr-1 is the closed record of the original 20 October lock and of the register row; it is not the record of the relock. The three cases locked on 20 October (a trip at each group's peak induced current, a disruption during an ongoing discharge, and the fastest quench with the FDUs inserted) are withdrawn.

The sequence is fixed by the lead's ruling of 21 October 2026. A fast discharge is never triggered by a disruption. It is triggered to protect the coils, on quench detection. The PF and CS currents it removes end plasma control, so a disruption follows the trip. Every case therefore starts with the FDU trip at t = 0, on the interlock sequence §5 carries: the converter to inversion, the PMS, the bypass and the breaker, then the counter-pulse and the resistor. The disruption onset is placed after the trip. IDM gives no delay between the trip and the loss of plasma control, so the onset is bounded at three instants, stated in the record as an assumption:

  • during the interlock delay, before the vacuum breaker separates, which is worst for the interrupted current because the induced current adds before the breaker opens;
  • at the resistor's insertion;
  • during the resistive decay, which adds to the resistor voltage and the energy each unit absorbs.

Losing the PF currents removes vertical control as well, so a vertical displacement event is the representative consequence. Each onset therefore runs one slow-quench VDE, with a fast-quench major disruption as the bound on the current-quench rate. The trip set is the one the interlock defines. If IDM does not say whether a single coil's quench discharges only that coil or the whole PF and CS system, both run as arms.

The switched coil circuits (converter, FDU and busbars) are driven by the disruption's plasma-linked flux through the same coupled plasma, passive and coil plant that §9 solves, not by coil EMFs computed separately and injected. All the current the plasma loses must reappear in the passive structure and the coils, and the transient circuits must carry that transfer. If the switched owner cannot take a prescribed plasma flux source through NovaPlant's ports, the section names the owner change it needs, and that change goes to the switched owner's holder and merges before any case runs, as the switched-circuit bracket-recursion fix did.

The plasma is imposed, not solved, from the ITER disruption database through §9's machinery. The cases come from the DINA-2010 design-basis set (100500–100533, which cites IDM documents 2PN3CN and 2MZWJR). Its largest coil current changes match 3M9D27's table in size: PF2 9.6 against 9.37 kA, PF4 6.7 against 6.6 kA, CS1 5.9 against 5.05 kA per module. §9 — What a disruption induces on the coils: a major disruption and a VDE imposed on nova's passive structure

Show what a current quench puts on the superconducting coils by imposing two stored 15 MA disruptions on nova's grid and solving only the passive structure's response; the plasma is never solved. This is the machinery §6 runs its FDU cases on, and its animation is the report's demonstration of the disruption database. The cases are from the DINA-2010 design-basis set in ITER_DISRUPTIONS (DD 4.0.0, HDF5, citing IDM 2PN3CN and 2MZWJR):

  • Major disruption, 100500/1: downward, thermal and current quench together, 80–20 % current quench in 30 ms, 0.33 s stored.
  • VDE, 100501/1: downward, halo fraction 0.42, the plasma displaced before its quench (magnetic axis from 0.53 to −3.69 m), 80–20 % current quench in 93 ms, 0.90 s stored.

The thermal quench, the displacement and the current quench are identified from the stored data (stored energy or temperature, magnetic axis height, plasma current), not assumed.

What the stored equilibria hold, checked on 20 October 2026 in every slice of both cases:

  • profiles_2d ψ on a 33 × 65 rectangular grid whose extent moves from slice to slice, present in every slice but the last;
  • no jφ, and no one-dimensional ψ, p′ or FF′;
  • no per-slice plasma current (summary carries it), and no boundary_separatrix (DD4);
  • the boundary outline and magnetic axis are present, and slice times are at the IDS level.

So the plasma is read through nova's own routines and nova is not edited here:

  • the topology of each slice from raw ψ through nova's contour tree (nova.equilibrium.topology.read, contour_tree.build_contour_tree) under the stored COCOS;
  • the flux functions from the map through nova.equilibrium.map_extraction (apply_delta_star, extract_flux_functions), with each slice's receipt reported;
  • the current imposed on nova's grid through nova.imas.plasma_source.PlasmaSlice.prescribe and normalised to the stored plasma current.

A slice whose extraction receipt is unreliable is counted, and is imposed from apply_delta_star's jφ instead. A change nova would need is reported as a blocker naming it.

The passive structure is nova's ITER passive set, the conductors behind nova_plant's modes, solved in full in three arms:

  • Held: with the superconducting coils' currents held, it gives the EMF each supply must absorb to hold its current.
  • Freewheeling: with the coils at zero voltage, it gives their current change.
  • Regulated: each supply on its averaged converter under its current controller (design_pi on supply_plants, as scripts/iter/current_controllers.py builds it, not DINA's controller), holding its pre-disruption current, at the register's converter voltage limits, with CS1 as its series pair. This is the arm the lead asked for: the voltage each coil actually receives, with the converter effects. Today current_control.coupled_plant takes plasma flux on the coil ports only, so the converter owner first gains a full-source plasma input on every circuit, passive-state output and the CS1 series port. That change and the regulated rerun are one node, briefed as converter-disruption-voltages, dispatched once cold-test-current-controllers has merged in current_control.py. Until it lands, the held and freewheeling arms are reported as the two bounds and labelled as bounds.

The source is the whole-wall map throughout. Both cases replay on one common timebase, aligned at thermal-quench onset, with the same output times and the same end time. When a case's plasma is extinguished, its stored current reaching zero or its record ending, its plasma current goes to zero, and nova keeps stepping the passive and coil circuits to the common end. That end is long enough for the slowest passive decay to show.

§12 — Every FDU interrupts on its counter-pulse, as the design does

§11 found that, with the FDR stray in the build, every insertion peak grows as the solver step falls. The growth continues to 6×10−8 s, below the insertion owner's own scan, and lives in the stray branch alone: with no stray the rows are flat. The cause is in §5's builds, not the stray. scripts/iter/fast_discharge.py places no counter-pulse element in any FDU. It carries the counter-pulse only as a timing and as a margin, rated current over breaker current. So each breaker opens by chopping its full current, which is harmless with no stray and unbounded with one.

The design does not chop. Every PF and CS FDU interrupts its vacuum breaker at a current zero that the counter-pulse forces, with a pyrobreaker as backup (778SPD v1.0, pp. 9–10 and 38–41). The counter-pulse is 1.6 mF and 16 µH on every circuit (7JQSNL v1.3, Tables 3 and 5). Its initial charge Uco is:

  • 7.6 kV on every CS module;
  • 7.9 kV on PF1, 9.0 kV on PF2, 9.2 kV on PF3, 9.1 kV on PF4, 8.5 kV on PF5 and 8.0 kV on PF6;
  • against a rated 10 kV charge.

The snubber is two identical RC circuits in parallel, 4 mF in total (two 2,000 µF capacitors) and 0.1 Ω. It sits in parallel with the main breaker and pyrobreaker (778SPD §1.1.2.2.6, Table 1.1.2-4).

This section enters those values in src/power_convertor/registers/iter_supplies.json, each with its IDM source. Every FDU fast_discharge.py builds then carries its CounterPulse, fired on the interlock schedule §5 already uses, and its snubber at the main-breaker attachment. §11's voltage cells are then re-filled where they settle.

  • Every PF, CS and VS1-connected FDU interrupts at a breaker current zero that its counter-pulse forces. The breaker current at opening is within one step of zero, and a test reads it.
  • With the FDR stray in the build, every insertion peak settles within 1 % between the last two step halvings over the insertion window. §11's terminal, resistor and arm voltage cells are filled at the settled step, with their moves against §5's receipt and any 778SPD or rating crossing called out.
  • Negative control: with the counter-pulse removed from one FDU, its insertion peak again fails to settle.
  • The counter-pulse margin is restated as the breaker current against Uco/√(L/C), the most current the pulse can zero (76 kA for CS, 92 kA for PF3), alongside the rated-current figure.
  • The energy over-sets are re-stated on the new build. Any row that moves is called out.

§ Decisions

Do we run disruption cases to qualify the FDUs (§6)?

Lead's ruling, 21 October 2026, superseding the bounded set locked on 20 October. A fast discharge is never triggered by a disruption: it is triggered on quench detection to protect the coils, and the loss of the PF and CS currents it causes ends plasma control, so a disruption follows the trip. Every case starts with the FDU trip at t = 0 on the interlock sequence (about 0.45 s from trip command to resistor insertion). The disruption onset is bounded at three instants, an assumption because IDM gives no delay from trip to loss of control: during the interlock delay before the vacuum breaker separates, at resistor insertion, and during the resistive decay. Each onset runs one slow-quench VDE and one fast-quench major disruption from the DINA-2010 design-basis set (100500-100533), imposed through §9. The 20 October cases (a trip at peak induced current, a disruption during an ongoing discharge, the fastest quench with the FDUs inserted) are withdrawn.

Held, though §5 and §9 have both closed. The switched owner's plasma input reaches the coil ports only. nova_plant.plasma_input_matrix, which into_switched uses, is −Lc−1 on the coils, with zeros on every passive mode. That is the coil-only interface §9 found in coupled_plant and closed there at 846ac2e3. §6 needs the same full-source option on into_switched: a plasma flux rate on every coil and passive mode, through the joint linkage.

Two things stand before it:

  • shared-coil-supply-model §6 is moving the plant source into nova_plant.py and is held on nova's linkage repair. The pinned plant's joint linkage is indefinite on VSU and VSL, and a full-source −L−1 on that linkage would grow.
  • The full-source option belongs to the switched owner's holder, the shared-model coordinator, and was sent there on 21 October.

§6 dispatches once the positive-definite plant is adopted and the option merges, with its positive control (a passive-only flux step moving the coils through the mutuals) and its default unchanged bit for bit.

The full-source option is now shared-coil-supply-model §10, "The switched path takes the full plasma source" (plan v166, 0e209509), so §6 depends on that section instead of the study-script refactor in its §6.

§10's done-when matches what §6 needs:

  • into_switched(..., full_source=True) takes a flux rate on every coil and passive mode, through −L−1 of the joint linkage;
  • off by default, the input matrix unchanged bit for bit;
  • positive control: a passive-mode-only flux step moves the coils as an analytic two-circuit case predicts;
  • negative control: removing the coil-to-passive mutual leaves them unmoved.

§10 waits on that plan's §9, the adoption of nova's repaired, positive-definite plant key, which in turn waits on nova:iter-passive-plasma-circuit §7.

JT-60SA has given a result §4 must carry (jt60sa-coil-circuit-model §17, merged 22fa0d89, review 94/120). The registered 2023 ripple filter and grounding do not explain the 2021-to-2023 change in coil-to-coil harmonic pickup. Eighteen single-converter coil-only pulses were scored through the composed plant with register values only, nothing refitted.

  • 7 of 120 lines fall within the 10 % rule, with a median absolute error of 90 %.
  • The predicted change between years is about 0.93 on almost every line.
  • The measured change runs from 0.08× to 74×, median 0.64, in both directions.
  • The design change attenuates lines by only 1–7 %.

For ITER, §4 carries harmonic idle-coil coupling as an empirical factor with measurement requirements:

  • tap wiring;
  • inter-coil ground return;
  • a supply-off baseline;
  • each idle supply's firing state.

A filter or grounding design change is never applied as a predictable correction to measured coupling. The detector-pickup estimates state this uncertainty beside each idle-coil line, and §8 carries it into the report. evidence

A bound from the TF cold-test synthesis (synthesis, a57aa493): the balanced earthing divider puts the neutral at 0 V, but EFD:DV7 measures 0.83–16.23 V on it. §4 bounds each terminal-to-ground voltage at V/2 + |Vneutral| rather than V/2, which reaches 96.6 V on the 30 kA cold-test discharge. It states which neutral offset it carries and where it comes from.

The deposit-side moves are 0.0002 % in a breaker current, 0.016 % in an arm's energy per unit and 0.041 % in a resistor's inserted energy, and they change no over-set on any build.
